verses.25:22: for in doing this you shall heap coals of fire upon his head, and the Lord shall repay you good things.
verses.25:23: The north wind rouses clouds, and a shameless countenance provokes a tongue.
verses.25:24: It is better to dwell upon a corner of a housetop than with a reviling woman in a shared house.
verses.25:25: As cold water is pleasant to a thirsty soul, so is a good message from a land far off.
verses.25:26: As if someone should stop up a spring and spoil an outlet of water, so it is unseemly for a righteous man to have fallen before an ungodly man.
verses.25:27: To eat much honey is not good, but one ought to honor glorious words.
verses.25:28: As a city with its walls cast down and unwalled, so is a man who does anything without counsel.
verses.26:1: As dew in harvest and as rain in summer, so there is no honor for a fool.
verses.26:2: As birds and sparrows fly, so a vain curse shall not come upon anyone.
verses.26:3: As a whip for a horse and a goad for a donkey, so is a rod for a lawless nation.
verses.26:4: Do not answer a fool in response to his folly, lest you become like him;
verses.26:5: but answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself.
verses.26:6: Out of his own ways he brings reproach upon himself who sends a word through a foolish messenger.
verses.26:7: Take away the walking of legs, and lawlessness from the mouth of fools.
verses.26:8: He who binds a stone in a sling is like one who gives glory to a fool.
verses.26:9: Thorns grow in the hand of a drunkard, and servitude in the hand of fools.
verses.26:10: All the flesh of fools is greatly tempest-tossed, for their consternation is crushed.
verses.26:11: As a dog when he returns to his own vomit and becomes detestable, so is a fool in his own wickedness who turns back to his own sin. There is a shame that brings on sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace.
verses.26:12: I saw a man who seemed wise to himself; yet a fool had more hope than he.
verses.26:13: A sluggard, when sent on a way, says, "There is a lion in the ways."
verses.26:14: As a door revolves upon its hinge, so does a sluggard upon his bed.
verses.26:15: Having hidden his hand in his bosom, a sluggard will not be able to bring it to his mouth.
verses.26:16: A sluggard appears wiser to himself than one who brings back a message in fullness.
verses.26:17: As one who seizes a dog's tail, so is one who presides over another's dispute.
verses.26:18: As those who heal put forth words to men, and the first one who meets the word shall be tripped up;
verses.26:19: so are all who lie in ambush for their own friends, and when they are seen, they say, "I did it in jest."
verses.26:20: With much wood a fire flourishes, and where there is no double-minded man, strife grows quiet.
verses.26:21: A hearth for coals and wood for fire, and a reviling man for the tumult of strife.
verses.26:22: The words of knaves are soft, yet they strike into the inner chambers of the inward parts.
verses.26:23: Silver given with deceit must be reckoned as a potsherd; smooth lips conceal a grievous heart.
verses.26:24: He who weeps over enemies consents to all things with his lips, yet in his heart he contrives words.
verses.26:25: If your enemy pleads with you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded; for seven evils are in his soul.
verses.26:26: He who conceals enmity frames deceit, and he covers up his own sins, though well known in councils.
verses.26:27: He who digs a pit for his neighbor shall fall into it; and he who rolls a stone rolls it upon himself.
verses.26:28: A lying tongue hates truth, and an unguarded mouth produces disorders.
verses.27:1: Do not boast about the things of tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day will bring forth.
verses.27:2: Let a neighbor commend you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.
verses.27:3: A stone is heavy, and sand is hard to bear, but the wrath of a fool is heavier than both.
verses.27:4: Merciless is fury, and sharp is wrath, yet jealousy endures no one.
verses.27:5: Open reproofs are better than hidden friendship.
verses.27:6: More trustworthy are the wounds of a friend than the willing kisses of an enemy.
verses.27:7: A soul that is full scoffs at honeycombs, but to a soul in want even bitter things appear sweet.
verses.27:8: Just as when a bird flies down from its own nest, so a man is brought into bondage when he is estranged from his own places.
verses.27:9: By ointments and wines and incense the heart is gladdened, but the soul is shattered by calamities.
verses.27:10: Do not forsake your friend or your father's friend, and do not enter the house of your brother when you suffer misfortune; better is a friend nearby than a brother dwelling afar.
verses.27:11: Become wise, son, that your heart may rejoice, and turn away from yourself words of reproach.
verses.27:12: A shrewd man hides himself when evils come on, but fools press forward and shall pay the penalty.
verses.27:13: Take away his garment, for he has passed by; an insolent man is he who ruins what belongs to others.
verses.27:14: Whoever blesses a friend in the morning with a loud voice shall be thought to differ in nothing from one who curses.
verses.27:15: Drops drive a man out of the house on a wintry day; likewise also a reviling woman out of his own house.
verses.27:16: The north wind is a harsh wind, yet by name it is called favorable.
verses.27:17: Iron sharpens iron, and a man sharpens the countenance of a companion.
verses.27:18: He who plants a fig tree shall eat its fruits, and he who watches over his own master shall be honored.
verses.27:19: Just as faces are not like faces, so neither are the minds of men.
verses.27:20: Hades and destruction are not filled; in like manner also the eyes of men are insatiable. An abomination to the Lord is one who fixes his eye, and the undisciplined are unrestrained in tongue.
verses.27:21: A test for silver and gold is refining by fire, and a man is tested through the mouth of those who commend him. The heart of a lawless man seeks out evil things, but an upright heart seeks knowledge.
verses.27:22: Even if you scourge a fool in the midst of an assembly, putting him to dishonor, you shall by no means remove his folly.
verses.27:23: Thoroughly know the souls of your flock, and set your heart upon your herds;
verses.27:24: for a man does not have power and strength forever, nor does he pass them on from generation to generation.
verses.27:25: Care for the green growth in the field, and you shall cut the grass; and gather the mountain hay,
verses.27:26: that you may have sheep for clothing; honor the field, that you may have lambs.
verses.27:27: Son, from me you have strong sayings for your life and for the life of your servants.
verses.28:1: An ungodly man flees when no one pursues, but a righteous man is confident as a lion.
verses.28:2: Because of the sins of the ungodly, disputes are stirred up, but a shrewd man shall quench them.
verses.28:3: A man bold in ungodly deeds oppresses the poor. Just as a violent and unprofitable rain,
verses.28:4: so those who forsake the law commend ungodliness; but those who love the law place a wall around themselves.
verses.28:5: Evil men shall not understand judgment, but those who seek the Lord shall understand in all things.
verses.28:6: Better is a poor man who walks in truth than a rich man who is false.
verses.28:7: A discerning son keeps the law, but he who shepherds debauchery dishonors his father.
verses.28:8: He who multiplies his wealth by interest and excessive gains gathers it for him who shows mercy to the poor.
verses.28:9: He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, he himself also has made his prayer abominable.
verses.28:10: He who leads the upright astray in an evil way shall himself fall into ruin, and the lawless shall pass through good things and shall not enter into them.
verses.28:11: A rich man is wise in his own estimation, but an understanding poor man shall condemn him.
verses.28:12: Through the help of the righteous there is great glory, but in the places of the ungodly men are captured.
verses.28:13: He who covers over his own ungodliness shall not prosper, but he who declares reproofs shall be loved.
verses.28:14: Blessed is the man who fears in all things out of reverence, but he who is hard of heart shall fall into evils.
verses.28:15: A hungry lion and a thirsty wolf is he who, being poor, rules as a tyrant over a needy nation.
verses.28:16: A king lacking in revenues is a great oppressor, but he who hates unrighteousness shall live a long time.
verses.28:17: He who becomes surety for a man under a charge of murder shall be a fugitive and not in safety. Discipline a son and he shall love you, and he shall give adornment to your soul; you shall by no means obey a lawless nation.
verses.28:18: He who walks righteously is helped, but he who walks in crooked ways shall be entangled.
verses.28:19: He who tills his own land shall be filled with bread, but he who pursues idleness shall be filled with poverty.
verses.28:20: A trustworthy man shall be greatly blessed, but the evil man shall not go unpunished.
verses.28:21: He who does not respect the faces of the righteous is not good; such a one will sell a man for a morsel of bread.
verses.28:22: An envious man hastens to become rich, and he does not know that a merciful man shall prevail over him.
verses.28:23: He who reproves a man's ways shall have greater favor than he who flatters with the tongue.
verses.28:24: He who casts off father or mother and thinks he does not sin, this one is a partner of an ungodly man.
verses.28:25: An unfaithful man judges rashly, but he who trusts in the Lord shall be well cared for.
verses.28:26: He who trusts in a presumptuous heart, such a one is a fool; but he who walks in wisdom shall be saved.
verses.28:27: He who gives to the poor shall not be in want, but he who turns away his eye shall be in great distress.
verses.28:28: In the places of the ungodly the righteous groan, but in their destruction the righteous shall be multiplied.
verses.29:1: Better is a man who reproves than a stiff-necked man, for when he is suddenly set aflame, there is no healing.
verses.29:2: When the righteous are praised, peoples shall rejoice; but when the ungodly rule, men groan.
verses.29:3: The father of a man who loves wisdom rejoices, but he who feeds harlots shall destroy wealth.
verses.29:4: A righteous king raises up a land, but a lawless man tears it down.
verses.29:5: He who prepares a net before the face of his own friend casts it around his own feet.
verses.29:6: For a man who sins there is a great snare, but the righteous shall be in joy and in gladness.
verses.29:7: A righteous man knows how to judge for the needy, but the ungodly does not understand knowledge, and the poor man has no discerning mind.
verses.29:8: Lawless men set a city ablaze, but the wise turn away wrath.
verses.29:9: A wise man judges nations, but a worthless man, when angry, is laughed to scorn and does not cower.
verses.29:10: Men who partake in bloodshed hate a devout man, but the upright shall seek out his soul.
verses.29:11: A fool brings forth all his fury, but a wise man holds it in reserve little by little.
verses.29:12: When a king listens to an unjust word, all those under him are lawless.
verses.29:13: When a creditor and a debtor meet one another, the Lord keeps watch over them both.
verses.29:14: When a king judges the poor in truth, his throne shall be established for a testimony.
verses.29:15: Blows and reproofs impart wisdom, but a straying child puts his parents to shame.
verses.29:16: When the ungodly are many, sins multiply; but when those fall, the righteous become greatly afraid.
verses.29:17: Discipline your son, and he shall give you rest, and he shall bestow adornment upon your soul.
verses.29:18: There shall by no means be an interpreter for a lawless nation, but he who guards the law is counted blessed.
verses.29:19: A stubborn servant will not be disciplined by words; for even if he understands, yet he will not obey.
verses.29:20: If you see a man hasty in words, know that a fool has more hope than he.
verses.29:21: He who lives in luxury from childhood shall become a servant, and in the end he shall grieve over himself.
verses.29:22: A wrathful man stirs up strife, and an angry man digs up sins.
verses.29:23: Arrogance humbles a man, but the Lord upholds the humble-minded with glory.
verses.29:24: He who shares with a thief hates his own soul; and if, when an oath is put forth, they hear and do not report it,
verses.29:25: fearing and being ashamed before men, they are tripped up; but he who trusts in the Lord shall rejoice. Ungodliness brings a downfall upon a man, but he who trusts in the Master shall be saved.
verses.29:26: Many wait upon the faces of rulers, but from the Lord comes justice for a man.
verses.29:27: A righteous man is an abomination to the unrighteous, and a straight path is an abomination to the lawless.
verses.30:1: Fear my words, son, and having received them, repent. Thus says the man to those who believe in God, and I cease.
verses.30:2: For I am the most foolish of all men, and the discernment of men is not in me.
verses.30:3: God has taught me wisdom, and I have known the knowledge of the holy ones.
verses.30:4: Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has gathered winds in a bosom? Who has wrapped up water in a garment? Who has laid hold of the ends of the earth? What is His name, or what is the name of His children?
verses.30:5: For all the words of God are refined by fire, and He Himself shields those who revere Him.
verses.30:6: Do not add to His words, lest He reprove you and you become a liar.
verses.30:7: Two things I ask of You; do not take away favor from me before I die:
verses.30:8: put far from me a vain and false word; do not give me wealth or poverty, but appoint for me what is needful and sufficient;
verses.30:9: lest, being filled, I become false and say, "Who sees me?" or, becoming poor, I steal and swear by the name of God.
verses.30:10: Do not deliver a servant into the hands of a master, lest he curse you and you be destroyed.
verses.30:11: An evil offspring curses his father and does not bless his mother.
verses.30:12: An evil offspring judges himself righteous, yet has not washed away his going forth.
verses.30:13: An evil offspring has lofty eyes, and lifts himself up with his eyelids.
verses.30:14: An evil offspring has swords as his teeth and knives as his jaw-teeth, so as to consume and devour the humble from the earth and their needy from among men.
verses.30:15: The leech had three daughters loved with love, and these three did not satisfy her; and the fourth was not content to say, "Enough!"
verses.30:16: Hades, and the passion of a woman, and Tartarus, and earth that is not satisfied with water, and water and fire shall by no means say, "It is enough!"
verses.30:17: The eye that mocks a father and dishonors the old age of a mother—may the ravens from the valleys pluck it out, and may the young of eagles devour it.
verses.30:18: Now there are three things impossible for me to understand, and the fourth I do not know:
verses.30:19: the tracks of a flying eagle, and the ways of a serpent upon a rock, and the paths of a ship sailing the sea, and the ways of a man in youth.
verses.30:20: Such is the way of an adulterous woman, who, when she has acted, washes herself and says she has done nothing wrong.
verses.30:21: On account of three things the earth is shaken, and the fourth it cannot bear:
verses.30:22: if a servant becomes king, and a fool is filled with food,
verses.30:23: and if a maidservant casts out her own mistress, and if a hated woman obtains a good husband.
verses.30:24: Now four things are the smallest upon the earth, yet these are wiser than the wise:
verses.30:25: the ants, which have no strength, yet they prepare their food in the summer;
verses.30:26: and the rock badgers, a tribe not strong, who make their own homes in the rocks;
verses.30:27: the locust is without a king, yet it marches forth in good order at a single command;
verses.30:28: and the lizard, supporting itself with its hands and easily caught, dwells in the strongholds of kings.
verses.30:29: Now there are three things that go smoothly on their way, and a fourth that strides well:
verses.30:30: a lion's whelp, mightier than the beasts, which does not turn aside nor cower before any beast;
verses.30:31: and a rooster walking boldly among the hens, and a he-goat leading a herd of goats, and a king addressing a nation.
verses.30:32: If you give yourself over to mirth and stretch out your hand with strife, you shall be dishonored.
verses.30:33: Press out milk, and there shall be butter; and if you squeeze nostrils, blood shall come forth; and if you draw out words, judgments and strifes shall come forth.
verses.31:1: My words have been spoken by God: the oracle of a king whom his mother instructed.
verses.31:2: What, child, will you keep? What? The utterances of God. Firstborn, I speak to you, O son: what, child of my womb? What, child of my vows?
verses.31:3: Do not give your wealth to women, nor your mind and livelihood to remorse.
verses.31:4: Do all things with counsel; drink wine with counsel. Rulers are prone to wrath; let them not drink wine,
verses.31:5: lest they drink and forget wisdom, and be altogether unable to judge the weak rightly.
verses.31:6: Give strong drink to those in sorrow, and wine to drink to those in anguish,
verses.31:7: that they may forget their poverty, and remember their toils no more.
verses.31:8: Open your mouth with the word of God, and judge all soundly;
verses.31:9: open your mouth and judge righteously, and decide the cause of the poor and the weak.
verses.31:10: Who shall find a valiant woman? For such a one is more precious than costly stones.
verses.31:11: The heart of her husband is confident in her; such a one shall not lack fine spoils;
verses.31:12: for she works good for her husband all her life.
verses.31:13: Winding wool and flax, she makes what is useful with her hands.
verses.31:14: She is like a ship trading from afar, and she gathers her livelihood,
verses.31:15: and rises while it is still night. She gives food to her household and tasks to her maidservants.
verses.31:16: Considering a field, she buys it; and from the fruits of her hands she plants a possession.
verses.31:17: Girding her loins strongly, she braces her arms for work.
verses.31:18: And she tastes that it is good to work, and her lamp is not extinguished all the night.
verses.31:19: She stretches out her forearms to what is profitable, and braces her hands to the spindle.
verses.31:20: She opens wide her hands to the poor, and stretches out fruit to the needy.
verses.31:21: Her husband is not anxious about those in the house whenever he tarries anywhere, for all those with her are clothed.
verses.31:22: She makes double cloaks for her husband, and garments of fine linen and purple for herself.
verses.31:23: And her husband becomes distinguished in the gates whenever he sits in council with the elders, the inhabitants of the land.
verses.31:25: She makes fine linen cloths and sells them, and girdles to the Canaanites. She opens her mouth heedfully and lawfully, and sets order upon her tongue.
verses.31:26: She clothes herself with strength and dignity, and rejoices in the latter days.
verses.31:27: The ways of her households are well-kept, and she does not eat the food of idleness.
verses.31:28: She opens her mouth to the wise in lawful order; her mercy raises up her children and they grow rich, and her husband praises her:
verses.31:29: "Many daughters have acquired wealth, many have done mighty deeds; but you surpass and excel them all."
verses.31:30: Charms are deceitful and the beauty of a woman is vain; for a discerning woman is blessed, and let her praise the fear of the Lord.
verses.31:31: Give to her of the fruits of her lips, and let her husband be praised in the gates.

notes.1:7: The Septuagint expands this verse with two additional clauses echoing Psalm 110:10 (LXX) ("good understanding belongs to all who practice it" and "piety toward God is the beginning of perception").
notes.1:17: Verse 1:16 is absent from the Greek critical text of Proverbs, and here the Septuagint reads "not unjustly" rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "in vain."
notes.1:22: Instead of the Hebrew question ("How long, O simple ones..."), the Septuagint presents a promise that the innocent shall not be put to shame for as long as they hold fast to righteousness.
notes.1:29: The Septuagint reads "the word of the Lord" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "the fear of the Lord."
notes.2:2: The Septuagint includes an additional third clause directing the hearer to apply the heart's understanding "to the admonition of your son."
notes.2:16: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text warns against a "foreign woman," the Septuagint renders the figure as "evil counsel" (kake boule), sustaining this metaphor through verse 19.
notes.2:18: "The earthborn" (ton gegenon) is the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew Rephaim, the departed shades of the underworld.
notes.2:20: Unlike the purpose clause in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Septuagint employs a contrary-to-fact conditional looking back at those who perished in verse 19.
notes.3:5: The Greek reads "in God" and "do not exalt yourself upon your own wisdom," whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "in the LORD" and "do not lean on your own understanding."
notes.3:6: In the Greek, the feminine pronoun ("her") and verb ("she may cut... straight") refer back to wisdom from verse 5 rather than to God.
notes.3:15: This verse and verse 16 contain expanded Septuagint clauses ("nothing evil shall oppose her. She is well known to all who draw near to her" and "out of her mouth righteousness goes forth, and she bears law and mercy upon her tongue") not found in the Masoretic Text.
notes.3:18: The Greek ends with the distinctive comparison "as upon the Lord," where the Masoretic Hebrew concludes with a beatitude on those who hold fast to wisdom.
notes.4:4: The Greek uses the plural relative pronoun ("who") and possessive ("our word"), presenting both father and mother together as the speaker's teachers.
notes.4:8: Verse 7 of the Masoretic Hebrew is absent from the Septuagint; the rare Greek verb pericharakoo ("fence about") pictures fortifying wisdom like a walled city.
notes.4:21: The Greek reads "your springs" (ai pegai sou), diverging notably from the Masoretic Hebrew "your eyes."
notes.4:27: The second half of the verse ("For God knows the ways on the right...") is a substantial Septuagint expansion absent from the Masoretic Hebrew.
notes.5:2: Greek 'the discernment of my lips commands you' differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('your lips may keep knowledge'), attributing the authoritative counsel directly to the teacher's speech.
notes.5:3: The Septuagint opens with the additional warning 'Do not give heed to a worthless woman' before describing the harlot's smooth speech.
notes.5:16: Unlike the Hebrew text, which is commonly read as a rhetorical question, the Septuagint introduces a direct prohibition ('Do not let waters overflow') and specifies 'your own streets.'
notes.5:19: The Septuagint expands the imagery of conjugal fidelity and uses the rare term pollostos ('greatly multiplied' or 'of great account') to describe the blessing of abiding in one's wife's friendship.
notes.6:6: The Greek form isthi here represents the imperative ithi ('go'), a standard Septuagint spelling; in verse 7 the ant is further described as having 'no farmland' rather than 'no chief.'
notes.6:8: The Septuagint includes an extended passage praising the bee's noble labor, health-giving honey, and exaltation through wisdom, which has no counterpart in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.6:11: After comparing poverty to an evil wayfarer and want to a good runner, the Septuagint adds a contrasting promise of an abundant harvest for the diligent.
notes.6:16: Instead of the Hebrew numerical saying ('six things... yes, seven'), the Septuagint links the following list directly to the lawless man of verses 12–15, who rejoices in all that God hates.
notes.7:1: The Septuagint includes a second couplet ("son, honor the Lord and you shall be strong, and besides Him do not fear another") not found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.7:6: Unlike the Hebrew text where the speaker looks out his own window, the Greek makes the strange woman the subject peering down from the window of her house into the streets.
notes.7:17: The Greek reads "saffron" for the couch and "cinnamon" for "my house," differing from the Hebrew sequence of myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.
notes.7:22: The Greek uses a rare word meaning "easily beguiled" (alluding to an easily trapped seabird) and likens the young man to "a dog to bonds" rather than a fool.
notes.8:1: Rather than the Hebrew rhetorical question ("Does not wisdom cry out?"), the Septuagint opens with a direct second-person statement: "You shall proclaim wisdom, that prudence may obey you."
notes.8:21: The Septuagint concludes this verse with an additional couplet promising that if Wisdom declares daily occurrences, she will also recount the things from eternity.
notes.8:22: The Septuagint renders the verb as "created" (ektisen) rather than "possessed," a reading central to early Christian Christological debates; compare the present-tense "begets" (genna) in 8:25.
notes.8:27: Where the Hebrew speaks of inscribing a circle on the face of the deep, the Greek reads "setting apart His own throne upon the winds."
notes.8:30: The participle harmozousa ("fitting things together" or "arranging in harmony") portrays Wisdom as a harmonizing artisan beside the Lord; verse 8:33 is absent from the Septuagint text.
notes.9:6: The Septuagint reads "that you may reign forever" (βασιλεύσητε) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "and live."
notes.9:10: The Greek reads "counsel of the holy ones" (βουλὴ ἁγίων) rather than the Hebrew "knowledge of the Holy One," and adds the concluding line concerning knowledge of the law.
notes.9:12: The Septuagint expands this verse with an extended poetic warning about one who relies on falsehoods, shepherds winds, and abandons his own vineyard (often numbered 9:12a-c).
notes.9:18: Greek γηγενεῖς ("the earthborn") renders the Hebrew Rephaim (shades of the dead), and πέτευρον denotes a springboard or trap-plank leading down into Hades. The Septuagint also appends the concluding exhortation to flee strange water (9:18a-d).
notes.10:4: The Septuagint begins with "Poverty humbles a man" (rather than the Hebrew "a slack hand") and includes an additional couplet contrasting a disciplined son with a fool.
notes.10:10: The second clause ("he who reproves with boldness makes peace") is distinctive to the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text repeats the closing line of verse 8.
notes.10:13: Following Codex Vaticanus and the main Septuagint critical text, this verse omits the opening clause ("He who brings forth wisdom from his lips...") found in other witnesses and the Hebrew, leaving the verb "strikes" syntactically linked to verse 12.
notes.10:26: The Septuagint reads "unripe grape" (ὄμφαξ) and "lawlessness" (παρανομία) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "vinegar" and "the sluggard."
notes.11:3: The Greek text speaks of regret left behind when a righteous man dies and the swift, welcomed ruin of the ungodly; verse 4 is absent from the Septuagint.
notes.11:10: In the Septuagint, verses 10 and 11 form a single two-line proverb, omitting the middle two clauses found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.11:26: The Greek optative expresses a wish that the grain-hoarder may leave his store behind to the nations, differing from the Hebrew reading where the people curse him.
notes.11:31: This Septuagint rendering is quoted nearly verbatim in the New Testament at 1 Peter 4:18.
notes.12:9: The Greek describes a humble man working for himself ("serving himself"), contrasting with the Hebrew reading of a man who has a servant.
notes.12:11: The Greek text includes an additional two-line proverb at the end of this verse warning against lingering over wine.
notes.12:13: The Septuagint adds a second couplet here; "whose look is gentle" literally renders the Greek idiom "who looks smooth things."
notes.12:18: The Greek text reads the nominative plural "swords" in vivid apposition to those who wound by speaking, rendered "like swords" for clarity.
notes.13:9: The second couplet ("Deceitful souls go astray...") is a distinctive Septuagint expansion not present in the Masoretic Text.
notes.13:12: The Septuagint renders the opening clause distinctively, contrasting wholehearted practical aid for those starting out with empty promises that merely lead into hope.
notes.13:13: The second sentence ("For a deceitful son...") is an additional Septuagint proverb absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.13:17: The Greek reads "a rash king" (basileus), differing from the Masoretic Text's "wicked messenger."
notes.14:10: The Greek portrays a sensitive heart whose soul feels sorrow yet avoids insolence in gladness, diverging from the Masoretic Text's statement about private bitterness and joy.
notes.14:15: The Greek word metanoia ("repentance") carries here the sense of thoughtful reconsideration or a wise change of mind.
notes.14:26: The Greek pronoun "His" and verb "leaves" naturally look back to "the Lord," though some take them as referring to the person who fears the Lord.
notes.14:30: The Greek likens a sensitive or easily agitated heart to a "moth" (ses) to the bones, whereas the Masoretic Text reads "envy is rottenness to the bones."
notes.15:1: The Septuagint opens with an additional clause ("Wrath destroys even the prudent") and uses the Greek participle hypopiptousa ("submissive" or "yielding") for the gentle answer.
notes.15:6: In the Septuagint, this verse incorporates the counterpart to Masoretic 15:5 together with an expanded doublet contrasting the strength of the righteous with the ruin of the ungodly.
notes.15:27: The Septuagint places the saying on mercy, faithfulness, and the fear of the Lord here, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text locates it at 16:6 (and similarly places counterparts to 16:7-9 in 15:28-29).
notes.15:33: The Greek reads "the beginning of glory shall answer to it" (referring to wisdom and instruction), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "before honor is humility."
notes.16:2: The Septuagint begins chapter 16 at verse 2, omitting counterparts to Masoretic 16:1, 3, 4, and 6 here and arranging several proverbs differently across chapters 15 and 16.
notes.16:15: The Greek reads "the son of a king" rather than "the king's countenance," and compares those acceptable to him to a "latter cloud" bringing late-season rain.
notes.16:16: The Septuagint translates the repeated noun as "nests" (nossiai) rather than "acquiring," reflecting a different reading of the underlying Hebrew consonants.
notes.16:21: Differing from the Hebrew, the Septuagint states that the wise and understanding are called "worthless" (phaulous), while those sweet in speech gain a greater hearing.
notes.16:33: Rather than the Hebrew saying about casting a lot into the lap, the Septuagint contrasts all things coming into the laps of the unrighteous with all righteous things that come from the Lord.
notes.17:6: The Greek adds a second proverb not present in the Masoretic Text; an obol was a small ancient Greek coin of minimal value.
notes.17:12: The Greek differs markedly from the Masoretic Text's image of a bear robbed of her cubs, contrasting a discerning man's anxiety with the evil schemes of fools.
notes.17:16: The second half of the Greek verse corresponds to material placed later in the Masoretic Text (17:19b-20).
notes.17:19: In the Greek text, verses 19-21 are divided across clause boundaries, and verse 21 adds a closing contrast regarding a prudent son gladdening his mother.
notes.18:8: The Greek differs substantially from the Masoretic Text's saying about a whisperer, presenting instead a proverb on fear and slothfulness.
notes.18:10: The Greek reads "From greatness of strength," reflecting a different reading of the consonants underlying "tower of strength" in the Masoretic Text; "to it" refers grammatically to the name of the Lord.
notes.18:17: The Greek presents a courtroom maxim in which the righteous person begins by accusing himself, and "he is put to the test" (or "exposed") may refer to either the speaker or the adversary.
notes.18:18: The Greek reads "a silent man" where the Masoretic Text has "the lot."
notes.18:22: The Greek adds a second couplet contrasting the dismissal of a good wife with keeping an adulteress, and ends chapter 18 here without the two verses found at 18:23-24 in the Masoretic Text.
notes.19:7: The Greek text expands significantly beyond the Hebrew here, adding two further couplets on good insight and the consequences of persistent wrongdoing.
notes.19:11: Literally 'his boast comes upon transgressors,' reflecting a Septuagint rendering that differs from the Hebrew sense of overlooking an offense.
notes.19:13: The second clause ('vows from the hire of a harlot are not pure') is a distinctive Septuagint reading that diverges sharply from the Hebrew.
notes.19:15: The Greek term androgynaios denotes an effeminate or fainthearted man, yielding a distinct moral image from the Hebrew.
notes.20:9: In the Septuagint arrangement, the sayings corresponding to Hebrew 20:20–22 are placed here within verse 9, while verses 14–19 are omitted.
notes.20:11: The Greek syntax is notably terse, stating that the maker of false weights shall be fettered in his practices before abruptly contrasting a young man who associates with a devout person.
notes.20:13: The Septuagint reads 'to slander' (katalalein) rather than 'sleep,' and warns against being removed rather than coming to poverty.
notes.20:27: The masculine relative pronoun ('who') refers grammatically to 'the Lord' rather than to the neuter 'light' or the feminine 'breath.'
notes.21:9: The Septuagint reads "whitewashed rooms with unrighteousness" rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "contentious woman," depicting luxurious yet corrupt shared quarters.
notes.21:16: "Assembly of giants" translates the Greek phrase used across the Septuagint for the Hebrew Rephaim, the shadowy departed of the underworld.
notes.21:18: "Ransom" translates Greek perikatharma, denoting a purification offering or scapegoat given in place of another.
notes.21:30: The Septuagint reads "for the ungodly man," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "against the Lord."
notes.22:7: The Septuagint reverses the second clause relative to the Hebrew Masoretic Text, stating that household servants will lend to their own masters rather than that the borrower serves the lender.
notes.22:8: The Septuagint includes an additional couplet (often numbered 22:8a) beginning "God blesses a cheerful man and a giver," echoed by Paul in Second Corinthians nine seven.
notes.22:15: Unlike the Hebrew text, the Septuagint omits a verb for driving folly away and states simply that "the rod and discipline are far from him," with Greek paidia representing the common spelling of paideia ("discipline").
notes.22:20: "Threefold" renders the Septuagint's understanding of a debated Hebrew term, and "upon the breadth of your soul" amplifies the scribal image of inscribing counsel within.
notes.22:23: The Septuagint reads "you shall deliver your inviolate soul," promising security to the one who refrains from oppressing the poor rather than describing the despoiling of oppressors as in the Hebrew text.
notes.23:2: The Septuagint instructs the guest to put forth his hand knowing he must reciprocate in kind, differing markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's warning to put a knife to one's throat.
notes.23:5: The Greek text pictures the rich man (or his wealth) fitted with eagle's wings, alighting nowhere and returning to the house of his overseer or patron.
notes.23:7: The Septuagint likens the envious man's eating and drinking to swallowing a hair, reflecting a different reading of the underlying Hebrew consonants from the Masoretic Text.
notes.23:24: Verse 23 of the Hebrew Masoretic Text is absent from the Septuagint text of Proverbs.
notes.23:31: The vivid Greek idiom "more naked than a pestle" warns against gazing upon wine bowls and cups, differing from the Masoretic Text's description of wine sparkling in the cup.
notes.24:5: The Septuagint contrasts a prudent man with "a great tilled field," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of a man of knowledge increasing strength.
notes.24:9: Verses 9–10 in the Septuagint diverge substantially from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, linking the fool's death in sins with uncleanness staining the pestilent man until he fails in a day of affliction.
notes.24:22: The Septuagint includes an extended addition here warning against speaking falsehood to a king and depicting the king's tongue as a sword not of flesh and his wrath as an all-consuming flame.
notes.24:27: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "afterward," the Septuagint reads "follow after me," linking the rebuilding of one's house to following wisdom's instruction.
notes.24:34: The Septuagint compares oncoming want to "a good runner," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's image of an armed man.
notes.25:1: The Greek reads "unarranged instructions" (paideiai adiakritoi) and "the friends" (hoi philoi, a Hellenistic court title for royal counselors), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "proverbs" and "men" of Hezekiah king of Judah.
notes.25:10: The closing sentence ("Grace and friendship deliver...") is a Septuagint expansion not found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.25:13: The Greek text reads simply "a going out" (exodos, perhaps a respite from field labor or an outlet of water); some Greek manuscripts add "of snow," closer to the Hebrew "cold of snow."
notes.25:19: The Greek text reads "way" (hodos), differing by a single letter from "tooth" (odous, corresponding to the Hebrew "broken tooth").
notes.26:3: The Greek reads "a lawless nation" (ethnei paranomo), reflecting a Hebrew reading of "nation" (goy) rather than the Masoretic "back [of fools]" (gev).
notes.26:11: The second sentence ("There is a shame that brings on sin...") is a Septuagint addition paralleling Sirach 4:21 and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.26:18: The Greek reads "those who heal" (hoi iomenoi), departing markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's picture of a madman hurling firebrands and arrows.
notes.26:24: Translated directly from the Greek text as given ("weeping over enemies," apoklaiomenos echthrous, and "words," logous); some Greek manuscripts read "a weeping enemy" (echthros) and "deceits" (dolous).
notes.27:4: In the Greek text, 'jealousy' is the grammatical subject with 'no one' as object ('jealousy endures no one'), contrasting with the Hebrew rhetorical question about who can stand before jealousy.
notes.27:11: The Septuagint reads 'your heart' and 'turn away from yourself words of reproach,' whereas the Hebrew reads 'my heart' and answering one who reproaches the speaker.
notes.27:16: The Septuagint renders this verse with a Greek proverbial euphemism in which the harsh north wind is called 'favorable' (epidexios), differing markedly from the Hebrew text.
notes.27:27: The Septuagint concludes the chapter with 'strong sayings' for the son and his servants, whereas the Hebrew refers to sufficient goats' milk for sustenance.
notes.28:3: In the Septuagint, the closing clause of verse 3 ('Just as a violent and unprofitable rain,') forms the first half of a comparison completed in verse 4.
notes.28:15: The Septuagint reads 'a thirsty wolf' and 'being poor,' likely reflecting a variant Hebrew reading of 'poor' (rash) rather than 'wicked' (rasha).
notes.28:17: The opening clause warns against becoming surety for someone charged with murder, while the second sentence ('Discipline a son... lawless nation') is an addition distinctive to the Septuagint.
notes.28:22: The Septuagint reads 'a merciful man' (eleemon) where the Hebrew has 'want' (cheser), likely reflecting a reading of the closely similar Hebrew word for mercy (chesed).
notes.29:1: The Septuagint reads 'Better is a man who reproves than a stiff-necked man, for when he is suddenly set aflame, there is no healing,' differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which speaks of a man often reproved who stiffens his neck and is suddenly broken.
notes.29:7: The Septuagint includes a third clause not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text: 'and the poor man has no discerning mind.'
notes.29:14: The Septuagint reads 'for a testimony' (Greek eis martyrion), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonantal text than the Masoretic Text's 'forever.'
notes.29:25: The Septuagint presents a double rendering of this verse, joining the first clause seamlessly to the oath-breaking scenario of verse 24 and adding a second parallel saying that refers to God as 'the Master' (Greek despotes).
notes.30:1: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text opens with the proper names Agur, Jakeh, Ithiel, and Ucal, the Septuagint interprets these forms as common nouns and verbs, yielding an exhortation to fear the speaker's words and an address to those who believe in God.
notes.30:4: The Septuagint reads the plural 'His children' (Greek tois teknois autou), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the singular 'his son.'
notes.30:12: Greek exodos ('going forth') functions here as a euphemism for bodily filth or excrement, corresponding to the Hebrew term for filth.
notes.30:15: The Septuagint counts 'three daughters' and a 'fourth' rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'two daughters,' and in verse 16 expands the list of insatiable things to include Tartarus and water.
notes.30:19: The Septuagint reads 'in youth' (Greek en neoteti), reflecting an abstract noun vocalization of the Hebrew consonants rendered 'with a maiden' in the Masoretic Text.
notes.31:1: The Greek text does not name King Lemuel, instead introducing the passage as words spoken by God and the oracle of an unnamed king instructed by his mother.
notes.31:20: The Greek noun karpon ("fruit") can also mean "wrist" (an anatomical parallel to "hands" in the first clause), denoting either the produce she shares or the hand she extends to the needy.
notes.31:21: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text mentions snow and scarlet clothing, the Greek text states that her husband is not anxious about those in the house when he tarries away because all with her are clothed.
notes.31:25: In the Septuagint verse arrangement, material corresponding to Hebrew 31:24 and 31:26 is combined in verse 25 (with verse 24 omitted), and the traders are rendered specifically as "the Canaanites."
notes.31:31: The Greek text reads "fruits of her lips" (rather than "hands") and concludes with "let her husband be praised in the gates" (rather than "her works"), following verse 30's distinct exhortation that the discerning woman praise the fear of the Lord.
